title: My friend, 'HootsMaguire', wrote an interesting analysis of Polanski's "Rosemary's Baby". With his permission, I wanted to share it here.

commenti.body:
This is from the School of Kael.

It is not an analysis of the movie--interesting or not.  It is comments about the director, about the director's religion, about the director's wife, about a president of the US, about a criminal active in the 1960s, about how the movie was made, about other movies, and so on and on and on and on.  Other than perhaps one paragraph (out of about 20 or so), it avoids discussing what is actually in that movie.  So, how it can be an analysis of what is inside the movie, is beyond me.

It poorly "analyzes" the stuff outside the movie as well.

I rate this "analysis" an F for fail.

Right.  I do think a holistic analysis of an artwork does include examination of extrinsic information.  What I often see, however, is this extrinsic information as itself a holistic analysis.  It is not, and what gets ignored or overlooked is the artwork qua artwork, or basically everything *intrinsic* to the film.  Rarely (virtually never) is there a synthesis of the intrinsic and extrinsic.  For example, a recurring theme in the film *Alien* is sexual assault and forced pregnancy.  These themes are influenced by second-wave feminist advocacy for bodily autonomy, but how does the fear of rape/pregnancy manifest in the film’s visual language?  How do the themes influence the film’s cinematography or its editing?  

I think part of the issue is that there is simply a lack of education about film theory as a field separate from either English/drama and/or cultural studies.  Generally, people are taught to analyze films as though they are works of literature (focus on plot, characters themes, symbolism) and/or as cultural products (focus on political, ethical content), and not taught to treat cinema as its own medium and films as complex audiovisual artworks.

I value interpretations of a work which start with what is inside it, rather than those which start with what is outside it.

If a viewer starts with what is outside a work, he will force interpretations upon it, as agendas or theories.  He will move downward and inward.  In effect he will use the work as a data point in support of an agenda or theory he already accepts.  He will thus necessarily devalue the work relative to his "explanation" of it.  He will necessarily end where he begins--with the agenda or theory he forces upon the work.

If a viewer starts with what is inside a work, he will follow interpretive paths related to what he actually sees and hears in it.  He will follow wherever the movie seems to lead him.  He can then move upward and outward by abstraction and generalization, and so on.  What he learns about what is in the work may surprise or confuse him but in good and entertaining ways.  He may learn about himself.  He will not end where he begins.
